14.9.9.en: * The prophet grieved over the misery of our feeble state, in which man finds no rest in his life and loses everything at the onset of sudden death. For the Holy Spirit had declared to him that man does not rise for a long time, until He comes who does not sew what is old together with what is new, nor join new material to the old (Mt 9:16), but makes all things new, as He said: "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). For He is the Resurrection (Jn 11:25), the firstborn of those who sleep (Col 1:18; Rev 1:5), in whom we truly receive the privilege of the coming resurrection. But until now He alone has risen with an everlasting resurrection.

14.10.0.en: St. Ambrose As the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up [11].

14.10.1.en: * [As if the waters flow down from the sea, and the river dries up empty] [11]. The mind of man is a sea, and the thoughts of his mind are like the waves of the sea. Sometimes this sea is swallowed up by wrath, and by grace becomes calm, and runs from hatred to bitterness. But when man dies [the water flows down from the sea]... [and when the river is emptied it dries up]. Thus the soul withdraws and the body remains empty. For the body without life is like the bed of a dry river.

14.10.3.en: So man lieth down (sleeps), and riseth not.

14.11.0.en: Till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep [12].

14.11.1.en: The word "death" has been removed from the dictionary of the Church, and she no longer experiences it. Among her true members there are none who are dead, but all are alive, for she is the living mystical body of the Lord, and since the Head is alive, the members are alive.

14.11.2.en: She is one living Church, the body of one living Head, who knows no tearing apart, but all are joined through the generations in a unity that surpasses the limits of time.

14.11.3.en: We do not believe in two churches, a church of the living and a church of the dead, but in one Church, some of whose members have completed their striving and have departed to Paradise, waiting until we, their fellow servants, complete our striving and cross over to them, and all receive the reward on the day of judgment.

14.11.4.en: We are one Church, some of whose members have completed their striving, overcome and triumphed, some are still striving, and the rest will come in the generations to come, and all are one living Church, regardless of bodily meeting in this world.

14.11.5.en: With this view of faith, we do not look at the dead as dead but as those who have fallen asleep in order to awake. This is with respect to their bodies; as for their souls, they do not slumber or sleep. Their souls have rested from striving, toil and pain, but they are not separated from us, for our bond is not a bodily bond. We love them and they love us; we call them blessed for their striving, and they pray for us.

14.11.6.en: * [And man lieth down, and riseth not, till the heavens be no more] (Job 14:12). This seems to mean until the heaven becomes new. For "there shall be a new heaven and a new earth" (Isa 65:17) LXX, as it is written. For what passes away is old, and what is old will be changed.

14.11.7.en: Listen to the Psalmist who says: [In the beginning, O Lord, thou hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the work of thine hands. They shall perish, but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed] (Ps 102:25-26). We too are able to weave the garment, for what is old passes away, but what is new is taken by force: "and from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force" (Mt 11:12).

14.11.8.en: The (Jewish) synagogue passed away with a few, and the Church seizes it by the thousands. Perhaps the meaning is also that the heaven now appears to pass away, since it is mingled with cloud, mist and the darkness of night, and with the dawning of a day of golden-red color it appears in manifold, multiplied colors. "And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light" (Rev 22:5), as John said. Or another says: "Woe to those who sew cushions, and are ground with the souls of the people" (Ezek 13:18) LXX.

14.11.9.en: St. Ambrose * [The man who lies down (in death) does not raise himself. As long as the heavens stand, (his members) are not joined together, and he does not rise from his sleep.]

14.11.10.en: By calling death a sleep, Job clearly presents to us the hope of the resurrection... He says that we do not raise ourselves as long as the (visible) heavens stand. This is a testimony that [the heaven shall be rolled together as a scroll], as Isaiah says, [and all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the moon shall be darkened, and the stars shall fall, as the leaf falleth off] (Isa 34:4; Mt 24:29). Then, when the trumpet is sounded (Mt 24:30-31; 1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16), the angels raise us from death as from sleep, clearly at the command and signal of God. For you will find these words of the Lord set at the time when He speaks with His disciples about His coming... And as He announces the appearance of the sign of His cross at His coming, He added: [He shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet](f)...

14.11.11.en: As for us, let us listen attentively to the saying: "They are joined together." It declares how, when the heavens pass away (Mt 24:35), we shall have the resurrection. Then there will be a place for the resurrection of the members, which are now separated and scattered on the earth, and have returned to clay. Then they take back the breath at God's command (Ezek 37:10), "and are joined together." For the Creator does not make for us another body, but in every respect it is the very same actual body. In any case, it will not be of the same character, but will rise in incorruption and immortality. He raises it, and as Paul says: [this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality] (1 Cor 15:53).

14.11.12.en: As Job thinks on this and contemplates the glory of the future and eternal life, as well as the lowliness of the present life, he holds fast to the idea of transformation from this swiftly passing life, and in hope of the life to come we hear him say: "Oh! if only someone would keep me from Gehenna!"

14.11.13.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [So man lieth down, and riseth not.] This seems very hard: why do we toil and strive, if we do not afterward find the reward of the resurrection?

14.11.14.en: How is it said, "he riseth not," when it is written: [We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed](g). And also: [If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable]. And the Truth Himself says: [All that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation] (1 Cor 15:51, 19; Jn 5:28-29). But the previous text adds: [till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep]. So it is clear that they will not rise until the heavens no longer exist; if the end of the world does not come, the human race does not awake to life from the sleep of death...

14.11.15.en: Furthermore, let us notice why, after first calling man dead, he then points to him as not dead but asleep, and that he will not rise again from his sleep until the heavens are broken up, which means nothing other than that we should understand clearly that, in likeness to the tree that revives again to life, he points to man as a dead sinner, that is, one in whom there is no life of righteousness. But when he speaks of the death of the body he prefers to call it not death but sleep. Surely he teaches us hope in the resurrection, in which man quickly rises from sleep; he will rise in a moment at a sign from his Creator, rising from the death of the body.

14.11.16.en: For the word "death" terrifies those of weak minds, but the title "sleep" is not frightening. Therefore, when Paul gives instructions to his disciples he says: [I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him again] (1 Thess 4:13-14).

14.12.0.en: O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me [13]!

14.12.1.en: Job longs for the grave as a place in which to hide for a time from the wrath of God. Here his aim differs from what he had before, when he was asking for death and the grave (Job 7:9; 10:18-21). He attributes what has befallen him to the wrath of God, because he had learned that the righteous man is always blessed and calamities do not befall him as they do the wicked.

14.12.2.en: In the midst of his bitter sufferings he desires death, knowing that he will go down to Hades, but only for a time, awaiting the work of divine salvation, so that the wrath will pass and he will enjoy the glorious resurrection.

14.12.3.en: Although Job groans over the weakness of human life on earth, as weaker than the life of a tree, yet in the midst of his sufferings he desires to hide in the grave to rest from pain and never to return to it. Job understands that death is a hiding in the grave, whose keys are in the hand of God, who opens it for His children to enter, and then brings them out again on His great day.

14.12.4.en: As Job looks at the bodies of the believers in the grave, he sees that there are still traces of wrath, until, when the body rises and enjoys glory, every trace of wrath comes completely to an end, and thus the power of death is destroyed.

14.12.5.en: Bodies enter the graves until the appointed time of coming out to the new, eternal life, just as Noah and his family entered the ark and God shut him in, not only to preserve them from destruction but to bring them into the new world, as though the days of the grave were better than the present days.

14.12.6.en: St. Ambrose sees in this passage (Job 14:13-17) that God spoke in Job and made known by the Holy Spirit that the Son of God would not only come upon the earth but also descend into Hades to raise the dead, and that what actually happened in his days was a testimony to the present things and a model of the things to come.

14.12.7.en: * What a wonderful passage this is, strengthening us concerning the resurrection!

14.12.8.en: How this passage appears in harmony with the words of the Lord that we read in the Gospel! He says: "Then shall they begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us" (Lk 23:30). For the wrath of the Lord will appear at the end of the world. Therefore the righteous Job preferred to rise at the judgment, and not at the time of the wrath of the Lord, which will be terrifying even for the righteous.

14.12.9.en: [That thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me] (Job 14:13). Job is understood to prophesy that he will rise at the time of the Lord's passion, as is clear from what is stated at the end of the book (Job 42:17) LXX, where the Septuagint reads [it is written that he will rise with those whom the Lord raises]. Yet he does not cease to lament, and the more he realizes that the resurrection awaits him, the more his longings increase to flee from this life. For he sees himself delivered into the hands of his adversaries, and falling under the power of the evil one.

14.12.10.en: St. Ambrose * [You who defend me in hell] [13]. Before the coming of the Mediator between God and men, every person, even if his life was pure and approved, undoubtedly went down to the prison of hell. Man, who fell by his deed, became unable by his deed to return to the rest of Paradise. For it is recorded that a flaming sword was set at the entrance of Paradise after the sin of the first man, which was called [the turning](h), until the day comes in which it turns...

14.12.11.en: [Until you keep me hidden until your wrath is completely past]. For the wrath of Almighty God accomplishes its power every day, so that those who live unjustly are swallowed up by fitting punishments...

14.12.12.en: In this matter we must know that the expression "wrath" does not befit the divine Being, since there is no agitation in the simple nature of God. For it was said to Him: [But thou, O master of power, judgest in calmness, and orderest us with exceeding great care] (Wis 12:18). But because the souls of the righteous were one day freed by the coming of the Mediator from the places of hell, which are not places of punishment, the righteous man foresaw it and asked, saying: [Appoint me a time, when You will come and remember me].

14.13.0.en: So may the blessed Job, since he knows this coming of our Savior to hell, ask for what he had already foreseen would happen in the future. Let him say: [And do You appoint me a time in which You will remember me], and he continues: [Do you think that a dead man will live again?] [14]

14.13.1.en: When our Lord was near His passion He spoke with the voice of the weak, saying: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me" (Mt 26:39). And in order to remove their fear He took (the fear) upon Himself (on their behalf).

14.13.2.en: Again He showed the strength by obedience in saying: "nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." So it is when it threatens us... In weakness we must pray that (what we fear) may not be, but we are ready for the will of our Creator to be done, even if it is against our will.

14.13.3.en: After this example it is sometimes fitting for the strong to adopt the words of the weak, so that through their strong preaching the hearts of the weak may grow in strength. So when the blessed Job uttered words like one in doubt, saying: "Do you think that a dead man will rise again?" he immediately added a phrase that confirms the certainty of his faith, where he says: "All the days in which I now struggle, I wait till my change come" [14].

14.13.5.en: * [In a letter the saint sent to a young widow, whose husband had been a governor, in which he says:] For this death is not death, but a kind of migration and passing from bad to better, from earth to heaven, from among men to the angels and archangels, indeed to God Himself, who is Lord of the angels and archangels...

14.13.6.en: So as much as you grieve that God has taken a man who was so good and honored, you ought to rejoice that he has departed to a place of greater safety and honor, delivered from the dangerous troubles of the present life, since he is now in safety and great tranquility.

14.13.7.en: If we have no need to be told that heaven is far better than earth, how can we lament those who have departed from this world to the other world?!

14.13.8.en: If your husband had walked like those who live a shameful life that does not please God, it would have been more fitting for you to mourn and weep, not only at his departure, but even while he was alive here. But inasmuch as he is one of the friends of God, we ought to rejoice in him, not only while he is alive here, but also when he lies down at rest.

14.13.9.en: And since we ought to do this, listen to what the blessed Apostle says: "having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Phil 23:1).

14.13.10.en: St. John Chrysostom If a man die, shall he live again?

14.13.11.en: All the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come [14].

14.13.12.en: God has no pleasure in the death of man, but that he return to Him and live. This is what moves Job to endure all the days of his striving, until his present days are changed into the new eternal life.

14.13.13.en: Job's friends, as weary comforters, offered him hope of a return to what he had been, if he would confess his hypocrisy and his hidden evil, offer sincere repentance, and return to God. But Job comforted himself with this: that he considered himself as one dead, who does not return to life on earth again, saying: "If a man die, shall he live again?" Yet this does not move him to slackness or to despair, but he says: "All the days of my striving I will wait till my change come." What change does Job wait for? The one of which the Apostle Paul said: "the form of the body of our humility shall be changed" (Phil 3:21). This is the change: instead of dry bones cast in a field, his life becomes an exceeding great army (Ezek 37:10). Thus the soul with all its powers and the body with all its abilities become a glorious and great army of the Lord, sharing the glory of the Lord Christ. Of this the Psalmist sings: [my flesh also shall rest in hope] (Ps 16:9). This is the joyful exchange in which the corruptible puts on incorruption, and the mortal puts on immortality.

14.13.14.en: Job's question came: "If a man die, shall he live again?" The answer came in the affirmative through the Lord of glory Jesus and what is recorded in the books of the New Testament (Jn 11:23-26; 1 Cor 15:3-57).

14.13.15.en: * [If a man must die, shall he rise, having completed the days of his life...? I wait until I exist again] (Job 14:14). He calls the resurrection a new existence... Job knew the arena not by words of praise uttered by the tongue, but by deeds. The words of praise were his sicknesses, his sores and his wounds. He was completely naked, and he was more splendid than one who wears garments embroidered with gold. For his bed on which he lay was a heap of refuse, yet he was more radiant than those who take delight in gold and precious stones. For God speaks with him personally, and the angels are at his side, and all creation proclaims the glory of the wrestler, who without stretching out his hands brings down the enemy.

14.13.16.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "For in that he died, he died unto sin once" (Rom 10:6).

14.13.17.en: He died not because He is mortal by nature, but He died in the body to put an end to sin. And He is alive in His life that does not pass away, as God.

14.13.18.en: Ibn al-Salibi * Because He is the Lover of mankind, He welcomed death, without which the world would have perished in its sins.

14.13.19.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * He was buried alone, but He raised all; He descended alone to lift us all; He bore the sins of the whole world alone to cleanse all in His own person, and as the Apostle says:

14.13.20.en: [Cleanse your hands, then, and be purified] (Jas 8:4); for Christ, who has no need of cleansing, was cleansed for our sake.

14.13.21.en: St. Ambrose * Be crucified with Christ, be put to death with Him, be buried with Him, that you may rise with Him, and be glorified with Him, and reign with Him.

14.13.22.en: St. Gregory the Theologian Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee.

14.14.0.en: Thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands [15].

14.14.1.en: God in His justice rejects disobedience and does not accept iniquity (Job 17:14), but as He orders salvation He longs for man, the work of His hands.

14.14.2.en: In the midst of distress Job cries out to God, as though God did not hear him, but when the time of the resurrection comes, God calls him to rise and Job answers; he meets God, who longs for the work of His hands, as Job bears the reflection of the splendor of God's glory upon him.

14.14.3.en: * [You ask me, and I will answer you] [15]... As long as we are subject to corruption we cannot answer our Creator by any means, seeing that corruption is far from incorruption, and there is no likeness fitting for our answer. Concerning this change it is written: [when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is] (1 Jn 3:2). Truly we shall answer God, who calls; at the command of "the supreme incorruption" we shall rise in incorruption. And because the creature cannot qualify for this by himself, but this is accomplished by the gift of Almighty God alone, namely to be changed to the glory of surpassing incorruption, therefore he rightly added: [You will stretch out Your right hand to the work of Your hands]. It is as though he were saying in plain words: for this reason Your corruptible creature is able to be held fast in incorruption, because he is lifted up by the hands of Your authority and kept by the grace of Your care. For the human creature, by this alone, being a creature, inherits in himself a collapse downward from what he is, but man receives from his Creator that he is bound to be lifted up to what is higher than himself by contemplation, and to hold fast incorruption in himself. He is lifted up to firmness in unchangeableness by the right hand of his Creator.

14.15.0.en: Who can estimate the generosity of the divine mercy, that it brings man after sin to the height of such glory? God takes into account the evil things we do, but in His compassion He forgives them in mercy. And so it is added: [For now thou numberest my steps, and passest over my sins] [16].

14.16.0.en: 16 For now thou numberest my steps: dost thou not watch over my sin? 17 My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity. 18 "And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place. 19 The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth; and thou destroyest the hope of man. 20 Thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth: thou changest his countenance, and sendest him away. 21 His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them. 22 But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn."

14.16.1.en: For now thou numberest my steps!

14.16.2.en: Dost thou not watch over my sin [16]?

14.16.3.en: The wise man says: "For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings" (Prov 5:21).

14.16.4.en: * [You number my steps, not one of my sins escapes You] [16]. He says: I want to be saved, because I am the work of Your hands, and not because I am righteous in any way, nor because I demand justice from You, nor that You should forget my iniquities, for it is not possible for any offense to escape You.

14.17.0.en: St. John Chrysostom My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity [17].

14.17.1.en: The Lord says: "Is not this laid up in store with me, and sealed up among my treasures?" (Deut 32:34).

14.17.2.en: This is about the joyful day of judgment, but now it seems to Job that God numbers his steps and seals up his transgressions as in a bag, as the papers of accusation are sealed against the accused. Job feels as though God scrutinizes every act Job performs and records all his sins against him, and all his iniquities are reckoned against him.

14.17.3.en: * [You seal up my transgressions, as if in a bag, but You heal my iniquities] [17]. Our transgressions are sealed up as in a bag, since whatever we do by outward conduct, if we do not wash it away by repentance, is kept in the secrecy of God's judgments as in a hidden place, until one day it appears from the bag of secrecy into the openness of judgment. It was also said by Moses: [Is not this laid up in store with me, and sealed up among my treasures? In the day of vengeance I will repay for them] (Deut 32:34). But if we are crushed by the blow of discipline for the evils we do, and grieve over them with repentance, then He "seals up" and "heals" our iniquities, so that He leaves nothing here for which we are not punished, nor is anything kept for which we shall be punished in the judgment...

14.17.4.en: So with the iniquity of His persecutor (Saul of Tarsus), whom He cast to the ground, He did this to him: He sealed and healed, saying of him to Ananias: [he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel: for I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake] (Acts 9:15).

14.18.0.en: And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place [18].

14.18.1.en: While the three friends reproach Job because, instead of repenting and returning to God, he accuses God of injustice in their eyes, Job makes clear that if weakness has come upon him, and he seems like one who has lost his hope, it is from the weight of the blow. He is like the mountain, which in spite of its firmness crumbles, and like the rock, which does not move, but under stress is removed from its place, and like the stones which successive drops of rain wear away and which the floods sweep off. So he likens himself to the mountain, the rock and the stones... But the trial is exceedingly severe!

14.19.0.en: The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth [19].

14.19.1.en: In the midst of his sufferings Job wrestles between his inability to bear the pain and his hope of enjoying the eternal reward. He has revealed his hope of an exchange and change even of his body, but he fears that this hope may be shifted by the length of the affliction. For we see that with the passing of time some mountains crumble, the rock is removed from its place, and the stones are worn by the water that falls on them continually and are swept away by the floods like the dust of the earth. He cries out that his patience may not last.

14.19.2.en: * He likens the ruin of man in this way... There are two kinds of trials:

14.19.3.en: One kind passes through the mind, even of a good man, and happens suddenly. He is tried suddenly, so that, not expecting what happens, he is seized with dizziness and falls to the ground and does not see his fall.

14.19.4.en: And there is another kind that comes little by little in the mind, and with good suggestions corrupts the resisting soul, not by its excessive extremity but by its insistence it corrupts the powers of righteousness.

14.19.5.en: When the first kind of trial is present, which makes a sudden attack and often brings the good man to the ground, it is said: [And surely the mountains fall to nothing, and the rock is moved from its place] [18], meaning the mind whose place was righteousness, and which by a sudden impulse is moved to sin.

14.19.6.en: Again, since there is another kind of trial, which pours itself quietly into the heart of man and wearies him, corrupting all the firmness of his steadfastness, it is said: [The waters wear the stones]. In this way, the soft flattery of the lust which is not forgiven absorbs the firmness of the soul, and the slow creeping in of the evil habit damages the steadfast and strong aim of the mind. Therefore it was added: [and by the washing the earth is eaten away little by little]. For just as by the overflowing of the waters the earth is eaten away little by little, so the evil habit creeps in by slight degrees, and even the strong mind is swallowed up. Rightly it was said: "and in the same way thou destroyest the hope of man"...

14.19.7.en: Let us see how David, "the high mountain," who was able to contemplate the great mysteries of God in the spirit of prophecy, collapsed in a sudden fall, when he desired and took another man's wife, and killed her husband at the cost of his army. Then the mountain fell in a sudden fall, when this mind, which was accustomed to dwell with the heavenly mysteries, was overcome by a sudden trial, and descended into such a terrible corruption...

14.19.8.en: Let us also see [the waters wearing the stones, and by the washing the earth eaten away little by little], in Solomon, who by his excess in relations with women and his association with them slipped down this road until he built a temple for idols, he who had earlier built a temple for God...

14.19.9.en: Thus the blessed Job sets forth both kinds of trial, whether that which happens suddenly in excess, or that which enters quietly and by a long way. Let him contemplate the falls of his fellows of creation (the mountains, rocks and earth), from which what happens outside can find a key for his meditations.

14.19.11.en: And thou destroyest the hope of man [19].

14.19.12.en: Thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth.

14.20.0.en: Thou changest (disfigurest) his countenance, and sendest him away [20].

14.20.1.en: Job asks for divine intervention before the hour of his death comes while he is in hopeless murmuring.

14.20.2.en: At the moments of death the face of man changes, either because of sickness or the state of emaciation that comes upon a man shortly before his death. Man loses his beauty, splendor and greatness, so that his relatives find that burying him is an honor to him. As Abraham says: [Give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight] (Gen 23:4, 8).

14.20.3.en: [You have shattered the hope of man]... Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem says that this is the reason David says: [Revive me, O God, for the waters have come to my soul] (Ps 69:1). For when our first parents Adam and Eve fell into disobedience they were driven out of Paradise and the sentence was pronounced: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return](i), and the earth brought forth thorns and thistles; what hope did Adam have after such a curse had come? Therefore Job continues his speech: [You have rejected him forever, and he is gone!]

14.21.0.en: His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them [21].

14.21.1.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that Job is looking at his father Adam, who has passed over to hell, so that he no longer knows what has befallen his children, that is, humanity, which is his offspring. "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mt 16:26).

14.21.2.en: * If the Lord's journey in the flesh had not taken place, the Savior would not have paid a price to death. He would not have destroyed the power of death by His might. If the body that was subject to death were one thing and the body that the Lord took another, then death could not have been stopped from carrying out its works, and the sufferings of the incarnate God would have been of no benefit; we who died in Adam could not have lived in Christ.

14.21.3.en: St. Basil the Great * We know Him as the firstborn of those who have rested, the firstborn from the dead. Without any dispute the firstfruit is of the same characteristics and nature as the rest of the fruits... Therefore as the firstfruit of death was in Adam, so the firstfruit of the resurrection is in Christ.

14.21.4.en: St. Ambrose Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this is the position of the souls that have not enjoyed salvation, but as for the souls of the righteous, or [the holy souls, since they see the splendor of Almighty God within them, they cannot imagine for a moment that something outside is unknown to them. But carnal persons, since they concentrate all their care on their children (on temporal matters), therefore Job declares that afterward they are ignorant of the things they love here with all their hearts, so that even if "their children are in honor or in disgrace, they do not know."]

14.22.0.en: But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn [22].

14.22.1.en: With his wonderful longing for death to escape the severe affliction, he fears the hour of death because it is dreadful, so that his soul seems to lament over the body that it is leaving.

14.22.2.en: * It was well said: [his soul within him shall mourn for him], for everyone who wants to rejoice in himself afterward comes, for the same reason, into woe, when he passes from the source of his true joy. For the true joy of the soul is the Creator. Therefore it is fitting for man to remain in eternal sorrow within himself because of leaving his Creator and seeking joy in himself.

14.22.4.en: To You I cry in the midst of my bitterness,
